EDITORIAL COMMENT
Genetics to the Rescue
Sophisticated Approaches Provide Critical Insights Into the
Determination of Lp(a) Levels *
Marlys L. Koschinsky, P HD,a,b Michael B. Boffa, P HDa,c
S
ince the ﬁrst report of lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) in
1963, basic scientists and clinicians have
endeavored to understand Lp(a) at all levels
from its basic biology to its role in cardiovascular dis-
ease (CVD) risk. Despite tremendous progress, many
unanswered questions remain about this enigmatic li-
poprotein. These encompass understanding how
elevated levels of Lp(a) contribute to disease pathol-
ogy at the molecular and cellular levels, how plasma
Lp(a) concentrations are determined, and how Lp(a)
should be used as a component of CVD risk
assessment.
A key challenge to understanding Lp(a) arises from
its extreme heterogeneity. Speci ﬁcally, the unique
apolipoprotein(a) (apo(a)) component of Lp(a) that is
covalently attached to apolipoprotein B in the Lp(a)
particle ranges considerably in size based on the
presence of a variable number of copies of a plas-
minogen kringle-like sequence. One of the 10 types of
kringle IV sequences in apo(a) (KIV1-KIV10), the KIV
type 2 sequence, is present in 3 to >40 identically
repeated copies encoded by differently sized alleles
of the LPA gene. A strong inverse correlation is
observed between the number of KIV repeats in
apo(a) and the concentrations of Lp(a) in plasma.
This, in turn, contributes to the wide range ( w1,000-
fold) of Lp(a) levels seen in the population.
It is therefore not surprising that the LPA gene is a
major contributor to plasma levels: up to 90% of the
variability of Lp(a) levels can be attributed to
sequence variation in LPA,i np a r t i c u l a rt h eK I V 2c o p y
number variation ( 1). However, the story is not so
simple. It is well-established that substantial vari-
ability exists in levels of Lp(a) for a given isoform.
This has prompted investigators to consider genetic
variants and their impact on Lp(a) levels throughout
the range of isoform sizes.
The KIV2 domain, in particular, has been compar-
atively impenetrable to the discovery of mutations
due to technical challenges arising from its identically
repeated sequences; advances in next-generation
sequencing have allowed characterization of the
mutation burden in this region. In this issue of the
Journal , Schachtl-Riess et al. ( 2)i d e n t iﬁed a novel but
highly prevalent single nucleotide polymorphism
( S N P )( m i n o ra l l e l ef r e q u e n c y0 . 2 2 4 )w i t h i nt h eLPA
KIV2-encoding region ( þ4733G >A). In the GCKD
(German Chronic Kidney Disease) study cohort
(n ¼ 4,673) for which there is information on both
Lp(a) levels and apo(a) isoform sizes, this mutation on
its own reduced Lp(a) levels by 13.6 mg/dL (95% CI:
12.5-14.7; P < 0.0001) and explained 9.6% of the
variance in Lp(a) levels, after adjustment for age, sex,
estimated glomerular ﬁltration rate, and major iso-
form size. When present as a compound heterozygote
with a second KIV2 mutation ( þ4925G >A) previously
found by this group ( 3), Lp(a) levels were dramatically
reduced by 31.8 mg/dL (95% CI: 30.2-33.3; P <
0.0001).
As the þ4733G >A mutation is located 11 base pairs
upstream of the 5
0 boundary of exon 2 encoding KIV2,

messenger RNA splicing. In vitro assays using a
minigene showed that the mutation induces 2 aber-
rant splicing events that would likely reduce protein
expression. Indeed, the þ4733G >Am u t a t i o n ,
observed across the whole range of apo(a) isoform
sizes but particularly in medium to large isoforms,
inverted the isoform size do minance in many carriers
such that the larger isoform was the more abundant.
Next, Schachtl-Riess et al. ( 2) turned to the 1000
Genomes Project to evaluate whether the new variant
affected Lp(a) levels in different ancestry groups. In
the present study, the þ4733G >A mutation was found
in the European, Latin American (Admixed Amer-
ican), and South Asian continental groups, but it was
not detected in East Asians and was very infrequently
observed in Africans. Hence, this mutation, like
others characterized in the KIV2 region and elsewhere
in LPA,i sc o m m o ni ns o m ea n c e s t r yg r o u p sa n da b -
sent in others, indicating that it may play a role in the
different relationships reported between LPA allele
size and Lp(a) levels in these groups ( 4).
Finally, and most relevant to clinical medicine,
Schachtl-Riess et al. ( 2)u s e dt h eU KB i o b a n k
(n ¼ 440,234) to assess associations of the KIV2 mu-
tations with coronary artery disease (CAD); to do this,
they had to identify proxy SNPs present in the Bio-
bank data set in strong linkage disequilibrium with
each variant. Likely carriers of þ4733G >Ah a da9 %
reduction in risk for CAD (HR: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.93-
0.89), whereas apparent þ4733G >A/þ4925G >Ac o m -
pound heterozygotes had a 12% risk reduction (HR:
0.88; 95% CI: 0.93-0.84). These ﬁndings are notable
because the reduction in Lp(a) attributable
to þ4733G >A alone is relatively modest: at
13.6 mg/dL, it is on a par with reductions of Lp(a) by
PCSK9 inhibitors that may reduce CVD risk over and
above that accruing from low-density lipoprotein
cholesterol reduction ( 5). The effect of genetic factors
on Lp(a) levels is lifelong, however. Clearly, it would
be informative to revisit Lp(a) risk for CAD in
different ancestry groups using large Mendelian
randomization approaches. To date, this has only
been performed in Northern European cohorts, and

understanding of Lp(a) as a causal risk factor for CAD
(1). Additional genomic analysis of LPA in other
ancestry groups will therefore be essential.
An important concept that is clearly illustrated by
the study of Schachtl-Riess et al. ( 2)c o n c e r n st h eu s e
of Lp(a) “threshold values ” to identify individuals at
risk for CAD. Based on their study, even relatively
modest lowering of Lp(a) had a signi ﬁcant effect on
lifetime risk. This re ﬂects the property of Lp(a) as a
continuous risk factor that has been shown in several
large studies ( 6,7). This may provide new ways to use
L p ( a )v a l u e sa sp a r to fa na l g o r i t h mt h a tr eﬂects a
linear relationship between levels and lifetime CAD
risk spanning the range of Lp(a) levels.
Another key point that is highlighted by the
present study concerns the potential role of isoform
size as an independent determinant of Lp(a) risk
after correction for Lp(a) levels. It appears from this
study, as well as from work of others, that when
corrected for Lp(a) concentration, apo(a) isoform
size per se is no longer a risk factor. However,

sian populations, and 1 study in a South Asian
cohort found that an SNP that predicted small iso-
form sizes but not elevated Lp(a) levels was asso-
ciated with risk for myocardial infarction ( 8). As

Impressive efforts from this research group have
demonstrated that the LPA KIV2 domain contains
many mutations, many of which likely result in null
alleles ( 3,9). What does this suggest about a possible
physiological role of Lp(a)? Owing to its high muta-
tion burden, it is tempting to speculate that apo(a)
may correspond to a transcribed pseudogene that
l a c k sap h y s i o l o g i c a lf u n c t i o n .T h i si sa l s os u p p o r t e d
by the wide range of plasma concentrations of Lp(a)
that are observed, including many individuals in
whom Lp(a) levels are well below the detection limit
of conventional assays.
As we await outcome data from the Lp(a)-HORIZON
(Assessing the Impact of Lipoprotein(a) Lowering
With TQJ230 on Major Cardiovascular Events in Pa-
tients With CVD; NCT04023552 ) trial that will test the
impact on risk for CVD events of speci ﬁcally lowering
Lp(a) using an antisense oligonucleotide (pelacarsen),
interest in the Lp(a) ﬁeld is growing. Additional ap-
proaches to speci ﬁcally lower Lp(a) are in various
stages of development incl uding small interfering
RNA–based strategies. In the interim, there remains
much work to be done from bench to bedside to
further re ﬁne our understanding of the nature of
Lp(a) risk and how to best identify individuals who
will achieve the greatest bene ﬁtf r o mt a r g e t e dL p ( a )
lowering. As more genetic variants are identi ﬁed that
modulate Lp(a) levels, it may be timely to consider
their use in machine learning algorithms as a tool to
characterize Lp(a)-attributable risk in patients.
Indeed, the large contribution of genetics to the
determination of Lp(a) levels, beyond LPA allele size,
clearly mandates genet ic characterization of
